content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper surveys the effectiveness of Complex-Valued CNNs (CV-CNNs) as opposed to Real-Valued CNNs (RV-CNNs) and presents the pitfalls that led to conflicting results in previous papers. This is mainly attributed to the difficulty of creating a matching RV-CNN for a given CV-CNN. The paper covers three different similarity measures, used for creating a matching RV-CNN network - (1) a similar architecture, (2) a similar number of parameters, and (3) a similar number of multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations. The paper continues by discussing the non-linearities in CV-CNNs as opposed to RV-CNNs and finally presents experiments, claiming that the effectiveness of CV-CNNs vary depending on the selected similarity measure for creating the matching RV-CNN, the depth of the network and the input data itself (i.e the importance of the magnitude/phase in the complex inputs).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The motivation for the paper is clear and important. The authors presented the pitfalls in previous comparisons and presented the importance in analyzing the different cases studied in literature and providing thorough and comprehensive results.
- The authors provide a significant number of results on a large amount of benchmarks.

Weaknesses:
- The overall text of the paper needs rephrasing. This will be discussed further in the following section.
- An entire subsection (2.4) is dedicated to the non-linearities, proving that non-linearities in CV-CNNs preserve magnitude/phase in complex numbers. This section seems to be unrelated to the rest of the paper. The authors do not provide an explanation for its purpose beforehand, and unfortunately the rest of the paper does not refer to the observations made there, nor do the results support the claim that the magnitude/phase preservation provides a benefit for CV-CNNs. For example, when comparing CV-CNN(2X) to RV-CNN(X), the performance gains in CV-CNN(2X) may be due to its ability to separate between the real and imaginary parts of the input (as in RV-CNN(C:2X) where the results are comparable).
- Table 1 presents a high-level summary of the results whereas the numeric results are presented using plots inside of figures 3 and 4. Sadly, the plots are barely readable due to their small size. This makes it very difficult for the reader to extract relevant information and understand the high-level claims made by the authors in Table 1. Some of the plots even contain an additional smaller plot which can not be read at all. 
- Regarding the chosen networks in the experiments - (1) ResNet5/8 are not standard architectures, and the reason for choosing them is not specified. I assume it is because ResNet18 is an over-parametrized network for CIFAR-10. In this case, why not use ResNet20/56, which are the CIFAR-compatible ResNets presented in the original ResNet paper? (2) The Vanilla CNN is composed of five-layers, and so is the moderately deep CNN (Mod-Deep). Most of the performance differences appear when using the Vanilla CNN, while for others the differences are subtle. The authors claim that increasing the depth of the network decreases the performance differences, but this does not explain the difference between the Vanilla and Mod-Deep versions since they have the same number of layers. Perhaps applying convolution layers resulted in a suitable network? This might point to the fact that the main concern is the capacity of the network to learn the task and not its depth. In any case, the differences are much less apparent when using a suitable architecture for the given task, so the lack of numeric results and/or readable plots makes it hard for the reader to follow the author’s claims.
- Results on MSTAR data have a high variance. Due to the fact the authors only ran 3 seeds, it’s hard to say, but they seem to be statistically significant. Can the authors comment on that?
As shown in the plots, it seems that using real-valued image data performs better than transforming the real data to complex values (and using any of the presented baseline models). This fact is overlooked in the paper, and it raises the question of the effectiveness complex representations have in these real-valued image tasks, and whether it might be better to test on more complex-input tasks.
- Maybe I’m missing something, but in the proof in section 2.4, the authors claim that the preservation of magnitude and phase implies the following: $tan^{−1}(f(x_i) / f(x_r)) = tan^{−1}(x_i / x_r)$, $f(x_i) = x_i; f(x_r) = x_r$. 
The first one refers to the phase, but shouldn’t the second one be $f(x_i)^2 + f(x_r)^2 = x_r^2 + x_i^2$?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The overall text and phrasing in the paper (and abstract) should be improved. There are a few technical issues the authors should correct as well, such as:
1. Some citations are not presented correctly. For example; Page 2, Lee et al., Subsection 2.2, Hirose. The ICLR format specifies when to use citet/citep. 
2. Authors refer to linear layers as a single input, single output layer. This can be confusing, as fully connected layers are commonly referred to as linear layers in literature.
3. Subsection 2.2 - The term “multiplication layer” is not defined in the paper.
4. Section 2.3 - “As a result, intuitively, based on similar network structure” - did the authors mean “...based on the similar number of MAC operations”?
5. Missing spaces, for example referring to Table 2 in section 2.3.
Authors use roman numerals for page numbering - I am not sure if this upholds the ICLR format guidelines.

- Additional clarity issues -
1. Why is ModReLU presented in Figure 2 if it is not discussed in the paper? (other than saying it preserves circular segments)
2. Under Equation (9), “B” is not defined.
3. The left part of the main figure presents the weights inside circles, although the circles commonly represent the activations when drawing neural networks.
4. Figure 3 in page 7 contains some of the experimental results, which are first discussed in page 9. Also, most of the experimental results are presented in figure 4, so why are only a fraction of them displayed in another unrelated figure?
5. Figure 3(a-b) uses the terms Mod-Deep CNN and Deep CNN, and is referred to before the terms are defined.

- Question: Regarding RV-CNN(X), presented in subsection (2.1) - how are both the real and imaginary values being fed into the network? When specifying the baselines, it states “..concatenated real and imaginary parts”. 

- Novelty: The authors tackle an important unresolved issue in the field and strive for a better understanding of the advantages of CV-CNNs. 

- Reproducibility: The authors did not provide code. Although the authors did make an attempt to help with reproducibility (for example setting a random seed), the details in the main paper are not complete for easy reproduction of the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper is well motivated and the authors present an interesting and important task, there are a few significant concerns, (1) the paper has some technical text flaws and requires additional work on phrasing, ordering, and presentation, (2) results are not well presented, which makes it hard for the reader to follow the author's main claims, (3) the network-depth claim should be revisited, and (4) additional complex-input tasks should be considered.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors motivate their work in that the existing literature in the area of Complex-Valued Convolutional Neural Networks (RV-CNNs) has contradictory conclusions on the value of these models for data domains that are inherently complex-valued, as compared to standard, i.e. Real-Valued CNNs (RV-CNNs), and this may be because of the different metrics and standards in deciding what models are directly comparable (e.g. in MACs, #parameters, etc). The authors propose to comprehensively empirically study various depths and architectures of CV-CNN models across a real-valued dataset (CIFAR-10/100), real-world complex-valued dataset (MSTAR), and CIFAR-10/100 modified to be complex-valued. They furthermore claim to show that ReLUs and max-pooling are not compatible with CV-CNNs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
* Paper is well-motivated, with it being important to understand the strengths/weaknesses of both real-valued and complex-valued approaches to data domains which are inherently complex.
* The empirical analysis that is outlined in the experimental method seems useful, with RV/CV-CNNs compared on a number of reasonable metrics with real-valued and complex-valued data.

# Weaknesses
* The analysis in Section 2 is either deeply flawed, poorly written, or both. The conclusion as written verbatim here is "Comparing equation 2 and equation 3, it is clear that complex-valued linear layer cannot represent the input-to-output mappings of the real-valued linear layer and vice versa". Clearly a real-valued number can be trivially represented as a complex number, and thus any complex representation can be learned with an appropriate real-value input (i.e. with imaginary component of 0) so this statement is trivially false. The issue with the author's analysis appears to be in comparing equation 2 ($f:\mathbb{C}^1 \to \mathbb{C}^1$) and equation 3 ($f:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$), which is an apples to oranges comparison. If instead they were comparing functions with the same input/output dimensionality, their analysis would clearly show this. I can only think maybe the authors are trying to compare a complex function and real function learned with the same number of parameters to make a point here, but both this comparison and the conclusion are incorrect.
* Lack of quantitative results in the main paper, certainly not living up to the "comprehensive" results/analysis promised. Table 1 is not quantitative or appropriate as the main results table of a paper. Even in the appendix, only Table 4 has any quantitative results, and this is a "sample" of the results.
* The claimed novel contributions of showing that both the standard ReLU activation function and max-pooling are problematic in CV-CNNs have already clearly been identified as a problem by the papers that proposed the alternative activation functions shown in this paper (i.e. ModReLU and CReLU) for complex neural networks, i.e. the uncited papers identified in the next point. For max-pooling Guberman et al. in 2016 and Trabelsi et al. 2018 (as cited) identified this problem, and suggested a generalized max-pooling operation for complex neural networks.
* No citations or definitions of ModReLU, CReLU, even though these are used in the paper. It appears ModRelu was proposed in "Unitary Evolution Recurrent Neural Networks" by Arjovsky et al. in 2016. CReLU in "Understanding and Improving Convolutional Neural Networks via Concatenated Rectified Linear Units" by Shang et al. in 2016.
* Unclear why it was decided to "augment" CIFAR to be complex, rather than just use another (real-world) complex-valued dataset. This could be better motivated.
* Figure 3 (c),(d) would be promising, but it seems for a "Deep CNN" MSTAR (the only real complex dataset) everything reaches 100% "accuracy" (training/validation/test, not clear), and so at best this seems inconclusive. This is not discussed in the results.
* Figures that do show some quantitative results are tiny and indecipherable. We are not told if accuracy in Fig. 3 is test/train/val.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper has serious issues with clarity & quality in particular, some already covered above:
* Trivially falsifiable mathematical statements (see above), it's not clear if this is due to issues with the writing or misunderstanding. 
* Many terms used without citation/definition (e.g. ModReLU, CReLU, VIBGYOR). ZRelu defined but not cited, as was defined by Trabelsi et al. in their work.
* Confusing usage of the terms of "linear layer" and "fully-connected layer", which are often used interchangeably in the NN community, here are defined to be different things. It seems in particular "linear layer" means a single neuron, which would rarely be a layer at all. Both seem to not include an activation function by the author's definition.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper is well-motivated (at least on the empirical analysis) in both the abstract and introduction, the empirical analysis results and presentation do not support the claimed contributions, and are far from comprehensive. The other contributions claiming to show problems with ReLU and max-pooling are not novel in that the authors themselves used ReLU and max-pooling alternatives for complex RNs already proposed by others who identified these issues. The analysis in Section 2 is flawed in writing and/or derivation and makes some troubling conclusions as written. I would encourage the authors to concentrate their future work on demonstrating the empirical analysis they claimed in future work, as I believe this could be useful if comprehensive and well presented, but unfortunately the current paper is simply not up to standards in results, writing and presentation.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper compares complex-valued (CV) CNNs and real-valued (RV) CNNs in fairer settings on several datasets.
The authors used RV CNNs that are comparable to a given CV CNN in architecture, the number of MAC operations and the number of parameters.
Empirical evaluations revealed that when CNNs are deep, both CV and RV CNNs achieved comparable performance.
They also show that when data have significant phase information, CV CNNs surpass RV ones.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

* The authors consider several settings for comparable RV CNNs to a given CV CNN.
Namely, RV CNNs with the same architecture, number of MAC operations, and number of parameters were considered.
I think this is a good and fair comparison.

* The authors used 11 datasets including transformed CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 to control the phase and magnitude of data, in addition to the standard CIFARs and a CV dataset of MSTAR.

## Weaknesses

* The empirical settings are limited, considering that the conclusion of this paper mostly relies on empirical results.
Especially, only small and shallow CNNs are considered.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity and Quality

The paper is generally well written. However, the figures are too small, for example, Figure 4 middle.


## Novelty

Considering various baseline RV CNNs may be new.

## Reproducibility

I cannot evaluate it.

## Comments

* Table 1 uses $>>$ or $<<$, but \ll ($\ll$) and \gg ($\gg$) are recommended.
* I would use radian in Figure 2 (B).
* "The line starting from "For CIFAR-10, ..." at the bottom of page 8 may be incorrectly broken?
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the experiments are limited, the paper shed light on the baseline RV settings in the research of CV neural networks, which I think is important.

content.title: ON COMPLEX-DOMAIN CNN REPRESENTATIONS FOR CLASSIFYING REAL/COMPLEX-VALUED DATA
content.TL;DR: We address the contradictory answers present in the literature for the following question: CV-CNN performs better or worse than RV-CNN for classification task?
content.abstract: This paper is about complex-valued CNNs (CV-CNNs) for computer vision that use  representations that are complex-valued instead of real-valued. We divide input data into three categories: inherently real-valued, inherently complex-valued, and  complex-valued obtained by transforming real-valued. We study the question whether complex-valued representation of CV-CNNs  offers any advantages over the commonly used  real-valued CNNs (RV-CNNs). For concreteness, we focus on the classification task.  The existing literature offers contradictory answers to our question. We find that this is mainly because (a) they seldom employ a common performance measure (e.g., CV-CNN compared against RV-CNN with similar network structure vs similar number of parameters) (b) diversity of evaluation datasets used are limited (e.g., datasets in which  magnitude information is more, less or as important as phase information) (c) less effort has been devoted to reduce the randomness in training between CV-CNN and RV-CNN.  Towards this, we propose  performance measures based on similar network structure, number of parameters and number of MAC operations. Also, we consider diverse datasets with varying magnitude/phase information, and deal with the randomness in training. As a result, we expect that any observed performance differences will be independent of the above disparities, and arise from the use of real vs complex representations.  Theoretically, we show that, unlike RV-CNNs,  CV-CNNs can preserve magnitude and phase through intermediate stages of processing. Our main experimental findings are the following. (1) As network depth decreases ---   the performance of CV-CNNs  improves  with respect to similar  network structure;   the performances of CV-CNN and RV-CNN having a similar number of parameters become more comparable; and   the performance of RV-CNNs improves with respect to similar number of MAC operations; (2) The above performance differences  diminish as the network depth increases. (3) With respect to data diversity,  performance depends on whether the dataset has dominant magnitude or phase, i.e., whether reconstruction error is lower using only magnitude or only phase.  If a complex-valued data has dominant magnitude,  instead of providing real and imaginary parts as input, providing the  magnitude part produces significant performance gain, whereas if the data has dominant phase, providing both real and imaginary parts is important. This holds true for different network depths.
